title: Frobenius reciprocity for rational induction of a character
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], $G$ an affine group scheme of finite type over $F$ [def-sc-group-scheme], and $H\subseteq G$ a closed subgroup scheme. For an affine $F$-scheme $X$ write $F[X]=\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$. Let $\chi:H\to\mathbf G_m$ be a group-scheme homomorphism, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$. Write $F_\chi$ for the one-dimensional rational $H$-module with $h\cdot a=\chi(h)a$. A rational $G$-module is an $F$-vector space $V$ with a coaction $V\to V\otimes_F F[G]$ satisfying coassociativity and the counit identity, and equivariant maps commute with coactions. Define the rational $G$-module
$$E_H(\chi)=\{f\in F[G]:f(gh)=\chi(h)^{-1}f(g)\text{ after every commutative }F\text{-algebra extension}\},$$
with action $(s f)(g)=f(s^{-1}g)$. For every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module $V$, evaluation at the identity gives an $F$-linear isomorphism
$$\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,E_H(\chi))\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_H(V|_H,F_\chi),\qquad a\longmapsto(v\longmapsto a(v)(1)).$$
Both Hom spaces consist of maps of rational group-scheme modules, with equivariance after every commutative $F$-algebra extension.

source.place: 22.29(a),(b) and 22.30, printed pp.470--471; regular-function rational induction, not abstract-group induction.

proof.text: Put $C=F[G]$ and $E=E_H(\chi)$. For affine products the coordinate algebra is the tensor product: algebra maps $B\otimes_F D\to A$ are exactly pairs of $F$-algebra maps $B\to A$, $D\to A$, so [def-weil-affine-spectrum] identifies its spectrum with the product by the universal property [def-pc-fibre-product]. Multiplication, inversion and identity of [def-sc-group-scheme] give pullbacks on regular functions; write $L:C\to C\otimes_F C$ for pullback along $(g,s)\mapsto s^{-1}g$, in that factor order. Associativity and the unit identity give $(L\otimes1)L=(1\otimes\Delta)L$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)L=1$. The semi-invariance condition is linear, so $E$ is a vector subspace. For $f\in E$, write $L(f)=\sum_i f_i\otimes a_i$ with the $a_i$ linearly independent (expand the finite span of the second factors in a basis). The identity $f(s^{-1}gh)=\chi(h)^{-1}f(s^{-1}g)$ gives $\sum_i(f_i(gh)-\chi(h)^{-1}f_i(g))\otimes a_i=0$. Applying coefficient functionals on the span of the $a_i$ gives the defining identity for every $f_i$, hence $L(f)\in E\otimes C$. Thus $L$ restricts to the required rational coaction on $E$. All displayed identities are identities of regular functions: they can be tested on universal points over the coordinate algebras of the relevant affine products. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum], an affine point is the corresponding algebra homomorphism, so testing on the identity homomorphism recovers the function itself. This works for nonreduced groups as well.

source.place: 22.29(a),(b) and 22.30, printed pp.470–471 (PDF pp.482–483); explicit coaction and inverse calculations supplied by Q27.

proof.text: Evaluation $\epsilon_E:E\to F$, $f\mapsto f(1)$, is linear. For any commutative $F$-algebra $A$, $h\in H(A)$ and $f\in E\otimes_F A$, one has $\epsilon_E(hf)=f(h^{-1})=\chi(h)f(1)$ by semi-invariance at $g=1$. If $a:V\to E$ is rational $G$-equivariant, its scalar extension satisfies $\epsilon_E(a(hv))=\epsilon_E(ha(v))=\chi(h)\epsilon_E(a(v))$. Therefore $T(a)=\epsilon_E\circ a$ belongs to $\operatorname{Hom}_H(V|_H,F_\chi)$, and $T$ is linear.

source.place: 22.29(a),(b) and 22.30, printed pp.470–471 (PDF pp.482–483); explicit coaction and inverse calculations supplied by Q27.

proof.text: For $\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}_H(V|_H,F_\chi)$ define $b_\lambda(v)(g)=\lambda(g^{-1}v)$. This is a regular function, not merely a function on $F$-points: if $\rho_V(v)=\sum_j v_j\otimes c_j$, then $b_\lambda(v)=\sum_j\lambda(v_j)S(c_j)\in C$, where $S$ is pullback by inversion. This formula defines an $F$-linear map $b_\lambda:V\to C$ independent of the tensor expression and commutes with scalar extension. For every $A$, $g\in G(A)$ and $h\in H(A)$, $b_\lambda(v)(gh)=\lambda(h^{-1}g^{-1}v)=\chi(h)^{-1}\lambda(g^{-1}v)$. Thus each $b_\lambda(v)$ belongs to $E$.

source.place: 22.29(a),(b) and 22.30, printed pp.470–471 (PDF pp.482–483); explicit coaction and inverse calculations supplied by Q27.

proof.text: For every $A$ and $s,g\in G(A)$, $b_\lambda(sv)(g)=\lambda(g^{-1}sv)=b_\lambda(v)(s^{-1}g)=(s b_\lambda(v))(g)$. These formulas apply to all $v\in V\otimes_F A$ by linearity. They imply equality of the two coaction maps: evaluate on the universal pair $(s,g)$, so the equality is in $C\otimes_F C$ for each $v$; the inclusion $E\otimes_F C\hookrightarrow C\otimes_F C$ is injective, since extending a vector-space basis of $E$ to one of $C$ gives a linear retraction. Consequently $b_\lambda$ is a morphism of rational $G$-modules. Its formula is also linear in $\lambda$.

source.place: 22.29(a),(b) and 22.30, printed pp.470–471 (PDF pp.482–483); explicit coaction and inverse calculations supplied by Q27.

proof.text: Finally $T(b_\lambda)(v)=b_\lambda(v)(1)=\lambda(v)$. Conversely, for an equivariant $a:V\to E$, $b_{T(a)}(v)(g)=T(a)(g^{-1}v)=a(g^{-1}v)(1)=(g^{-1}a(v))(1)=a(v)(g)$. This is valid after every algebra extension; taking the universal $g$ proves equality as regular functions. Thus $T$ and $\lambda\mapsto b_\lambda$ are inverse linear maps, giving exactly the asserted isomorphism.
